summary: At a median home price of $152,600 and a price-to-income ratio under 2.8, Alturas is one of the most affordable county seats in all of California — a statistic that genuinely startles anyone accustomed to coastal housing math. Sitting at roughly 4,370 feet in the high desert of the Modoc Plateau, this town of about 2,660 occupies a compact 2.9 square miles in a wide sagebrush valley where the Pit River passes through, framed by the Warner Mountains to the east and open rangeland in nearly every other direction — the kind of terrain that delivers enormous, unobstructed sunsets and winter nights cold enough to justify real insulation. The economy is anchored by county government, healthcare at the local hospital, ranching, and timber-related services; switching employers without a long drive is constrained simply because the private-sector job pool is small. Summers average highs around 85°F with 8.5 hours of daily sunshine, genuinely pleasant for hiking in the surrounding Modoc National Forest, while winters dip well below freezing and bring snow that can isolate the area — U.S. Route 395 and State Route 299 are the main lifelines, and the nearest city of any size is Redding, about three hours southwest. Rent at $781 a month is manageable against the $54,634 median household income, but a 23.3% poverty rate signals that wages, not just housing costs, define the affordability picture. Alturas is a place where geographic remoteness is not a side effect but the central fact of daily life — shaping everything from grocery options to career ceilings.
